# Diagnosing Two-Stroke Kill-at-Wide-Throttle Failures

A two-stroke engine stalling specifically under full load is a distinct failure mode that points directly to air-fuel mixture imbalance rather than general starting issues. Since your unit starts and idles smoothly, the ignition system, compression, and low-speed carburetor circuit are functioning correctly. The fact that the cylinder glows orange at high throttle confirms that combustion is occurring; if there were a catastrophic lean condition causing immediate detonation or overheating, you would likely see white smoke or hear a distinct knocking sound before it cuts out. However, a glowing port indicates hot exhaust gases escaping through an open valve or port while the engine is under load, which often signals a specific tuning issue.

The most probable cause for this symptom is a lean condition at wide-open throttle (WOT). In two-stroke engines, the carburetor's main jet is responsible for metering fuel when the throttle plate is fully open. If the mixture becomes too leanâmeaning insufficient fuel relative to the air intakeâthe engine will starve and cut out precisely when you demand maximum power. This explains why changing to a carefully measured fresh mix might not have solved it; if the carburetor jetting is mismatched for the specific engine or altitude, no amount of mixing ratio adjustment in the tank will compensate.

Check the air filter housing integrity first. Even if the filter element itself is clean, a compromised seal allows unmetered air to bypass the filter and enter the intake manifold directly. This extra, unmeasured air skews the air-fuel ratio lean at high RPMs where airflow volume is greatest. Inspect the gaskets around the filter mount and the throttle body for cracks or degradation. A visual leak test can be performed by starting the engine, letting it idle, and gently spraying carburetor cleaner or propane near suspected leak points while observing if the RPM drops; a drop indicates a vacuum leak.

Another critical factor is the exhaust system port alignment. You mentioned the cylinder can be seen through the exhaust port. While this is standard for many strimmers to allow cooling air flow, ensure that the exhaust muffler has not been modified or damaged in a way that alters backpressure. Excessive backpressure can cause unburnt fuel to wash oil off the cylinder walls, leading to scoring, but conversely, too little backpressure (a free-flowing exhaust) can reduce scavenging efficiency, potentially causing the engine to lose power and stumble under load. The orange glow you observe is simply heat transfer through the port; if the glow persists after the throttle is released, it suggests the cylinder head gasket may be failing or the ports are worn, allowing hot gases to escape past the piston ring before the exhaust valve closes.

If the engine continues to cut out despite a verified sealed intake and correct jetting, consider the spark plug condition under load. A weak spark or one that fouls easily under high heat can cause misfiring when the cylinder temperature peaks. Remove the spark plug and inspect the electrode for erosion or heavy carbon buildup. If the engine runs rich enough to glow but still dies, it could be a timing issue where the ignition points (if points) or CDI unit are failing to fire consistently at high speed.

While dismantling the carburetor is often the first instinct, verify the float level and needle valve adjustment before doing so. A float that sits too low will restrict fuel flow to the main jet, starving the engine exactly when you need it most. Adjusting the idle mixture screw can also help isolate whether the issue is purely in the main circuit or if the transition between idle and full throttle is abrupt due to a clogged emulsion tube.
